targets.title: The effects of reading material on social and non-social cognition.
targets.evidence_quote: We aimed to replicate and extend Black and Barnes’ (2015a) finding on narrative transportation, while approaching empathy as a trait construct.
targets.outcome_quote: Although these results did not replicate Black and Barnes’ (2015a) finding that literary fiction engenders higher narrative transportation than nonfiction, they did provide evidence that positive affect may be a central factor that undergirds the experience of narrative transportation into particular texts.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Explicit discussion comparison settles this published finding.

targets.authors: Hall, A. E., & Bracken, C. C.
targets.title: “I really liked that movie”: Testing the relationship between trait empathy, transportation, perceived realism, and movie enjoyment.
targets.evidence_quote: The first hypothesis was that trait empathy would be positively correlated with narrative transportation (Hall & Bracken, 2011; Taylor, 2015).
targets.outcome_quote: The correlation detected between trait empathy and narrative transportation supports and extends prior literature that has demonstrated similar results with films (Hall & Bracken, 2011; Taylor, 2015), as well as studies that have examined the relationship between some components of trait empathy and narrative transportation into written pieces (Bal & Veltkamp, 2013; Johnson, 2012).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Explicit discussion comparison settles this published finding.

reasoning: New sample explicitly retests the fiction-versus-nonfiction transportation finding and a specific prereported trait-empathy correlation, prospectively linked to Hall and Bracken and Taylor. Kidd and Castano supply materials and motivation; their theory-of-mind outcome is not tested. Bal and Veltkamp and Johnson are broader contextual comparisons, not the named primary hypothesis sources. Text excludes appended journal advertisements.
